title: Architectural Invariants of Feynman Graphs: A Green-Function Architecture Framework for Perturbative Quantum Field Theory
content: Perturbative quantum field theory is formulated in terms of Green functions and Feynman diagrams, which provide one of the most successful computational frameworks in modern theoretical physics. Besides their physical interpretation, Feynman diagrams are finite graphs endowed with rich combinatorial and topological structures. Existing mathematical descriptions include graph-theoretical invariants, Symanzik graph polynomials, and the Hopf-algebraic formulation of renormalization. However, these constructions characterize only specific structural aspects of perturbative graphs and no single invariant simultaneously describes propagation, interaction, holonomy, and recursive organization. In this work, we introduce a Green-Function Architecture framework for perturbative Feynman graphs. Every finite graph is assigned a canonical architectural coordinate (a,b,c,d) where the four coordinates quantify propagation, interaction, holonomy, and recursion, respectively. The recursion coordinate is defined intrinsically as the maximal nesting depth of one-particle-irreducible (1PI) subgraphs, thereby providing a graph-theoretical characterization independent of perturbative amplitudes. Based on these coordinates, we formulate the general theory of multiplicative architectural invariants and show that every invariant satisfying natural structural axioms possesses an exponential representation. The canonical Green-Function Architecture realization is then introduced through the Architectural Invariant Π(D)=2a(D) 3b(D) (3π)c(D) Ad(D)/8, with A=(1-1/3π)-1. Fundamental mathematical properties of the invariant are established, including graph-isomorphism invariance, multiplicativity, additivity of the logarithmic architectural complexity, and transformation laws under elementary graph operations. The proposed invariant is compared with established graph invariants including Betti numbers, Symanzik polynomials, and the Connes–Kreimer Hopf algebra. Finally, explicit examples from perturbative quantum field theory illustrate the computation of architectural coordinates and the associated invariant. The present work proposes an invariant-theoretic extension of the mathematical study of perturbative Feynman graphs. Rather than modifying quantum field theory, it introduces an additional structural invariant whose mathematical properties and possible physical significance provide a basis for future investigation.
